newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ merch trade reflects export growth - economists.
newsitem.headline: NZ merch trade reflects export growth - economists.

text.p: New Zealand merchandise trade data for July reveal an improvement in export performance, driven primarily from the commodity sector, Bankers Trust New Zealand economists said on Monday.
Earlier, Statistics New Zealand said the trade balance recorded a deficit of NZ$122.5 million in July, compared with a surplus in June of NZ$28.3 million.

The unadjusted value of exports was $1.82 billion, up 8.8 percent on June and 14.6 percent on July 1995. Imports were valued at $1.94 billion, up 18.1 percent on June and 8.4 percent on the year ago figure.
The trade balance for the year to July 1996 was NZ$552 million in deficit.

BTNZ said the commodity sector was the main factor behind the export growth, with dairy produce exports rising by 40 percent and fruit and nut exports by 22 percent in the July quarter against the year ago quarter.
Dairy produce exports were up $94 million in July, meat and edible offal were up $37 million and wool up $21 million.
BTNZ said an appreciating Trade-Weighted Index (up six percent in the last year) suggested an even larger increase in overall export volumes.
"The TWI has plateaud around 64-66 since early February. This pause in the currency's appreciation may have allowed exporters to adjust to its higher level," BTNZ said.
It added that on the flip side, imports were still posting healthy increases. As a partial indicator of domestic activity the rise in imports suggested the economy's slowdown was only gradual.

Bancorp Treasury Services economists said they had kept an eye on the growth of exports to ASEAN countries over the past few months. On an annual basis, these rose 18.5 percent in July, against 14 percent in June and 17.5 percent in May.
They said Malaysia, for example, took 25.2 percent more of New Zealand's exports in the July year, entering the top 10 countries for NZ exports.

"If we continue to grow our exports at this rate, the ASEAN destinations will have overtaken the EU destinations and the OECD destinations by the middle of next year in annual volume terms," Bancorp said.

"Currently the ASEAN countries only account for 8.2 percent of our total exports but at this growth rate could well challenge the APEC and OECD countries as our major export destinations by the turn of the century."
Bancorp added that competition was heavy, as the rest of the world had also recognised the opportunities that lay within the region.
